---
title: "Practical work 1"
subtitle: "DAI · A file processing CLI"
---

## What you will build

- A **command line tool**, written in Java with
  [picocli](https://picocli.info/).
- It reads **one file**, processes it, and writes **another file**.
- **You choose what it does.** Text, images, audio, encryption, metadata…
- In **groups of 3** (pairs allowed), over 4 sessions, then a
  presentation.

## Why this project

- Chapter 03: Maven, an executable JAR, unit tests.
- Chapter 04: charsets, buffering, `try`-with-resources, line endings.
- Chapter 02: issues, pull requests, reviews, signed commits.
- Next: the same code, reading from a socket instead of a file.

## Demo

```sh
java -jar target/my-cli-1.0-SNAPSHOT.jar \
  --input input.txt --output output.txt \
  --input-encoding UTF-8 --output-encoding US-ASCII \
  uppercase
```

```text
$ cat input.txt
Bonjour, comment ça va aujourd'hui ?

$ cat output.txt
BONJOUR, COMMENT ?A VA AUJOURD'HUI ?
```

You know why the `ç` is lost.

## What your CLI must do

- An **input file** and an **output file** as arguments, plus options.
- **At least two commands**, each with a help message.
- Files opened, read and written with the **Java I/O API** of chapter 04.
  Other libraries may process the data, not open the files.
- It uses **what the chapter teaches**: charsets, binary streams, or
  line endings.
- The **processing is separate** from the CLI, and tested.
- **Slightly more** than the course examples.

## Groups and idea

- **Groups of 3.** Pairs allowed. No group? Come and see us.
- Open a **GitHub Discussion** today, category *Show and tell*:
  - title: `[DAI {{< var year >}} Class <A or C>] PW1 - <names>`,
  - description: a few lines on what your CLI will do.
- We answer with a **go**, or with a suggestion to grow or shrink the
  scope.

## Sessions

| # | Milestone |
|---|-----------|
| 1 | Idea posted, repository ready, Maven and picocli skeleton. |
| 2 | Processing works: charset, buffering, resources. First tests. |
| 3 | Errors handled, example files, README. |
| 4 | Edge-case tests, README complete, PRs merged. |

Dates for your class are on the practical work page. Submission the
evening before the presentations.

## Grading

25 criteria, each 0, 0.1 or 0.2 point. Grade = points + 1 (max 6).

| Category | Weight |
|----------|-------:|
| 1. Git, GitHub and Markdown | 40% |
| 2. Java and Maven | 16% |
| 3. Java I/O | 24% |
| 4. Tests | 4% |
| 5. Presentation | 16% |

The full grid is on the [practical work page](../practical-work/pw1.qmd).
Read it **before** you start, not the evening before the deadline.

## What we look at most

- The files are read and written **correctly**: charset, buffering,
  resources closed, errors reported.
- The **README**: what it does, how to build and run it, with examples.
- **Tests** on the processing, separated from the CLI.
- A **team** history: issues, pull requests, reviews.

## Presentations

- **8 minutes** per group, computer and projector.
- Show the tool **running on real files**, including a failure.
- Explain the **what** and the **why**, not every line.
- Everyone speaks, everyone can answer questions about the code.

## Rules

- Everyone contributes, and everyone can explain the whole project.
- State your sources: internet, AI tools, ideas. Say what you used them
  for.
- Copying another group gives a grade of 1 to everyone involved.
- Late: 1 point per day.

## Keep it simple

> Write programs that do one thing and do it well.

- The Unix philosophy: small tools, working together, on text streams.
- KISS: *keep it simple, silly*. A tool that is too complex costs you
  points, it does not win them.
- Better a small tool that handles encodings and errors well, than a big
  one that crashes.

## Start now

1. Form your group.
2. Post your idea in the Discussions.
3. Create the repository, add everyone and the teaching staff.
4. `mvn` skeleton with picocli and two empty commands.

[Practical work 1](../practical-work/pw1.qmd) has everything: milestones,
dates, the full grid.
